evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[1]
evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 耳 (ear) and 德 represent the meaning and 𡈼 (tǐng) represents the sound.

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[2]
evidence.text: 聆也。从耳、㥁，壬聲。

evidence.field: hanzi.etymology_notes[3]
evidence.text:
Originally 𦔻, hence ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 耳 (“ear”) + 口 (“mouth(s)”) – to listen. Compare the top component of 聖.
Later, rewritten as phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *l̥ʰeːŋ, *l̥ʰeːŋs): phonetic 𡈼 (OC *l̥ʰeːŋʔ) + semantic 耳 (“ear”) + semantic 㥁 on the right.
The simplified version, 𠯸 (later stylized as 听), is totally unrelated to the original character and it originally means "smiling".
This is traditionally considered to have the same origin as 聖 (OC *hljeŋs, “to hear; wise; sage”) and 聲 (OC *qʰjeŋ, “sound”). Additionally, it may be also related to 聆 (OC *reːŋ, “to hear; to listen”) (Wang, 1982).
Outside connections unclear, although note Proto-Hlai *hliːŋ (“to hear (it said)”) from Pre-Hlai *(h)leːŋ (Norquest, 2007).
Derivatives:
* 廳 (OC *l̥ʰeːŋ, “hall, i.e. where hearings take place”)
* 廷 (OC *l'eːŋ, *l'eːŋʔ, “palace courtyard”).

evidence.field: B00294 听; Shuowen interpretation and meanings
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the received Shuowen explanation for 听: “smiling appearance; from 口, with 斤 as phonetic,” and cites Han Sima Xiangru’s Shanglin fu “亡是公听然而笑” as an example. It separately classifies tīng as a variant used for 聽. This supports a distinct old 听 word/graph and later overlap of the graph with 聽, but does not itself document when that overlap began.
evidence.title: [B00294] 听 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A03282 聽; variant record for 听
evidence.text: The 聽 record lists 听 among its variants and cites Song-Yuan vernacular character forms and the correspondence table for simplified characters as evidence. It explicitly reports “聽” written “听” in the simplified-character standardization. This supports classifying 聽 as the traditional counterpart and 听 as its standardized simplified form; it does not establish that the graph’s older “smiling” history derives from 聽.
evidence.title: [A03282-011] 听 (聽) - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.text: The entry independently reports the Shuowen definition of 听 as a smiling appearance, 口 + phonetic 斤, and Guangyun fanqie 宜引 and 牛謹. It displays two Middle Chinese categories, both rising tone. Its displayed contemporary Mandarin alternatives include tīng for the 聽-related use and yǐn for the smiling-word reading; those readings must not be conflated.

evidence.field: 聽 entry; paleographic account and ancient uses
evidence.text: The account describes oracle-bone forms of 聽 as ear with mouth, or ear with two mouths, interpreted as hearing sounds; it reports bronze forms with ear and mouth, and oracle-bone uses for hearing, hearing/handling government, and hearing political affairs, as well as names and ritual terms. evidence.field: 听; separate Chinese etymologies and historical phonology
evidence.text: The entry separates 听’s simplified use for 聽 from the older 听 word. It reports that the latter means laughing/smiling, gives Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese forms *ŋɡrɯnʔ and *ŋɡɯnʔ with 斤 as its phonetic-series label, and gives 斤 *kɯn, *kɯns in that same Zhengzhang system. This is a secondary transcription of a reconstruction system; the local Baxter–Sagart 聽 rows use a different system and do not support substituting those forms for Baxter–Sagart values.
evidence.title: 听 - Wiktionary

evidence.field: 聽; competing formation and loan account
evidence.text: The entry reports an early 聽 form 𦔻 as ear + mouth(s), later a phonosemantic analysis, and the proposal that 听 was stylized from 𠯸, a form with phonetic 厅, before being used for 聽. It also records the traditional Shuowen account as an alternative historical analysis. These are secondary-source assertions; the reviewed primary dictionary evidence establishes the separate old 听 entry and later simplification, but does not settle every step in the proposed 𠯸 → 听 graphic pathway.
evidence.title: 聽 - Wiktionary

evidence.field: 听; report on vernacular forms and proposed graphic corruption
evidence.text: The entry asserts that a Song-Yuan vernacular form 𠯸 used 口 with 厅 as phonetic, with 厅 itself a vernacular abbreviation of 廳, and that copying led to graphic assimilation as 斤. This is a specific corruption proposal, not demonstrated by a manuscript image in the inspected record. The Ministry of Education dictionary independently confirms Song-Yuan vernacular use of 听 for 聽, but does not verify the full proposed corruption sequence.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

Although CUHK indexes oracle-bone and bronze forms of 聽 and gives transcribed examples, glyph images were not visually inspected here. Exact earliest archaeological attestation and dating of each graphic variant remain unverified.

The evidence supports 口 as the semantic category for the old smiling sense and received Shuowen’s 斤-as-phonetic analysis. The separate histories of the 听 ‘smiling’ word and 聽 ‘hear/listen’ are established in the dictionaries, but the exact date and textual path by which the former graph began representing the latter word is not established by the sources inspected. No local row for a possible sound component 厅 was supplied, and no ancient pronunciation/name for the hall-related graph was independently recovered. The proposed 厅 phonetic intermediary therefore remains a graphic-analysis claim, not an independently verified sound reconstruction.
